answer: I would like to talk about someone whose imagination I find quite amazing. A creative person I really admire is a friend of mine who works as a graphic designer for an advertising agency in Dhaka. We were in the same year at university, although she was always more interested in art than in accounting. She designs logos, posters and packaging for all kinds of local brands, and she also paints in her spare time. What amazes me is how she can take a dull, ordinary brief and turn it into something genuinely [[striking]]. She seems to see possibilities that the rest of us simply miss. I have watched her sketch ideas that at first look random, then slowly come together into something clever and [[original]]. She is also fearless about experimenting, which I think is the heart of real creativity; she is not afraid to fail. Talking to her about her process is fascinating, because she draws inspiration from the most [[unlikely places]], like the painted rickshaws in our town or old films. Her work has this [[distinctive]] style that you can recognise instantly, which is quite an achievement in a crowded field. Honestly, spending time around her makes me want to be more imaginative in my own work, even if that only means designing a slightly better presentation for students. I think creativity like hers is partly a gift and partly relentless practice, and she has plenty of both. I genuinely believe she will have her own studio one day.

followUps.q: Do you consider yourself a creative person?
followUps.answer: Not especially, at least not artistically. I am more creative with words and ideas than with pictures. I would love to learn to draw, but I suspect I have no [[flair]] for it whatsoever.

followUps.q: Would you like to have some of her work at home?
followUps.answer: Definitely. She once gave me a small painting of the Jamuna at sunset, and it hangs in my room. I would happily buy more of her work if she ever decided to sell it.

note: Added who she is and what she creates (logos, posters, painting), a rickshaw-art detail and a closing line; replaced plain mark 'unexpected' with 'unlikely places'.
